rounds.prompt:
You are the final story-logic reader of a finished Swiss Standard German (ss, never ß — never dialect) children's picture book. You get the text of every page in reading order, as it will be printed. The text has already been proofread for spelling and grammar. Your only job is the story logic a careful parent, or the child listening, would trip over when the words are read aloud. Judge the text only.

The main character is: Janna. Every question that says "the main character" is judged against exactly that character, never against whoever the title names first.

VERSE FORM. This whole book is told in rhyming verse: rhyming couplets (AABB), each verse line on its own line of the page, a blank line between stanzas of two or four lines. This form replaces the paragraph shape and the sentence-per-paragraph rules for this book: a stanza is the paragraph, and a stanza of one sentence is fine. The lines have a steady beat a child can clap: every line has about four stressed beats (roughly 8 to 11 syllables), and the two lines of a couplet have the same beat and about the same length. A line is never a whole prose sentence with a rhyme word stuck on its end: when a thought is too long for one line, it is split over two lines or said more simply, and a long name or place is used where it fits the beat or left out of that line. When a page holds more than fits in a few stanzas, it says less in fewer words, never longer lines. Rhyme is only the FORM of the telling: the plot is an ordinary plot, and no character, game, rule or spell is built on rhyming. If the story idea gives a character a rhyming habit (it answers in rhyme words, it speaks only in rhymes), that habit is dropped: the character speaks ordinary words, and the story keeps its plot. Every couplet rhymes when read aloud in this language. The words stay plain words a child at the reading level already uses; word order stays the natural order of a spoken sentence, and no line is padded with a word, or made to say something odd, only to rhyme. Spoken lines stay in the cast's ordinary speech. You judge the story, not the verse: use this form only for the VERSE question.

# PAGES

--- Page 1 ---
Als Erste trat Melodi durch die Tür des gelben Bahnhofgebäudes in Dietikon. Draussen dämmerte es an diesem Herbstabend, und auf der Strasse warteten schon die Familien. Melisa folgte ihr und trug Jannas bemalte Laterne vorsichtig in beiden Händen.

«Polina!», rief Melodi. «Ballerina!», rief Polina und drehte sich einmal im Kreis. Neben ihr blieb ein Platz frei. «Der ist für Janna», sagte sie, aber Janna suchte drinnen noch ihren Mantel.

--- Page 2 ---
Drinnen wollten die Knebel nicht zugehen.
Janna konnte nicht länger stehen.
«Das dauert zu lange!», murmelte sie.
Dann rannte sie hinaus, so schnell wie noch nie.

Vor der Tür lag Laub, ein grosser Haufen.
Janna trat kräftig hinein im Laufen.
Ein silbernes Blatt hob sich im Abendlicht.
Janna starrte darauf und rührte sich nicht.

--- Page 3 ---
Aus dem Laub trat Silbermond, ein Einhorn mit silbergrauem Fell, und kam auf Janna zu. Sie wich einen Schritt zurück. «Geh!», sagte sie.

«Steh!», antwortete das Einhorn. Seine Stimme klang über den ganzen Platz.

Janna lief ein paar Schritte zur Seite, und Silbermond ging mit, dicht an ihrem Mantel. Am Ende der Bahnhofstrasse wurden die Lichter der Laternen schon kleiner.

--- Page 4 ---
Janna rannte durch das Laub zur Bahnhofstrasse, und Silbermond trabte dicht an ihrem Mantel mit. «Polina!», rief sie nach vorn. Es kam kein Reim zurück. Auf dem Trottoir sangen die Familien ein Laternenlied, und Jannas dünne Stimme ging darin unter.

Ein kleines Kind im Wagen zeigte auf das Einhorn und lachte. Die Eltern schauten nur den Laternen nach, denn nur Kinder konnten Silbermond sehen und hören. Janna drängte sich zwischen den Leuten hindurch. Neben Polina blieb der Platz leer.

--- Page 5 ---
«Weg!», rief Janna dem Einhorn zu. «Steg!», rief es zurück. «Fort!», rief sie noch einmal, und es antwortete: «Dort!» Silbermond blieb an ihrem Mantel, und die Erwachsenen drehten sich nicht um, obwohl die Reime laut über die Strasse klangen.

Vor der Kirche Sankt Agatha rückten die Laternen derweil zu einem Ring zusammen. Hinter ihnen stand der weisse Turm. Nur eine kleine Lücke war noch offen.

--- Page 6 ---
Auf dem Platz vor Sankt Agatha blieb Janna stehen. Die Laternen standen dicht beieinander, und jede war nur ein kleines Licht. Polina war die Kleinste, und über den Laternen war sie nicht zu sehen.

«Polina?», sagte Janna leise. Es kam keine Antwort. Sie presste die Lippen zusammen und rührte sich nicht. Silbermond legte den Kopf an ihre Schulter und blieb bei ihr.

--- Page 7 ---
Da hatte Janna eine Idee. Silbermond antwortete auf jedes Wort mit einem Reim, und seine Stimme war lauter als das ganze Lied. «Wenn ich ‹Ballerina› sage, reimt Silbermond ‹Polina›», dachte sie. «Dann hört Polina ihren Namen und ruft zurück!»

Janna wandte sich zu Silbermond und sagte laut: «Ballerina!»

--- Page 8 ---
«Polina!», reimte Silbermond, so laut, dass es über den ganzen Platz klang.

Polina hörte zwischen den Laternen ihren Namen. Sie sprang hoch und rief wie immer: «Ballerina!» Janna konnte Polina nicht sehen. Aber sie hörte den Ruf und wusste jetzt, wo Polina stand.

--- Page 9 ---
Melodi hörte Polinas Ruf und sah:
Die Lücke im Ring war noch da.

«Halt!», rief sie zittrig und hob die Hand.
Der Ring blieb offen, die Reihe stand.

Melisa hob Jannas Laterne hinauf.
«Janna, hier!», sagte sie darauf.

Janna sah das Licht und rannte hin.
Sie trat neben Polina, nun war sie drin.

Silbermond ging neben ihr her.
Melodi und Melisa staunten sehr.

«Ein Einhorn!», staunte Polina. «Oh!»
«Da bist du ja!», rief sie froh.

--- Page 10 ---
Nach dem Lied gingen die vier Mädchen zum Bahnhof zurück. Silbermond ging neben Janna, und niemand sprach viel. Am Laubhaufen vor der gelben Tür blieben sie stehen.

«Danke dir!», sagte Janna. «Bei mir!», antwortete Silbermond. Dann trat er ins Laub, und ein silbernes Blatt schwebte auf ihn hinab. Als das Blatt lag, war das Einhorn fort.

«Polina!», rief Janna. «Ballerina!», rief Polina und drehte sich. Janna drehte sich mit ihr, und beide lachten.

# QUESTIONS

Read the whole book once. Then answer these for the book as a whole. Each question has an id; use exactly that id in your answer.

OBSTACLE. Name the act on the page that removes the central problem and who performs it. It is a fault when a friend, an adult, luck or the problem itself removes it and the main character's own act (an idea, a choice, a brave or kind deed) is not what makes the difference. Helpers may help; the deciding act is the main character's.
STAKES. Is it said on the pages what the main character wants and what failing would cost? When a creature, an animal or another non-family figure drives the plot, is its reason (why it came, why it wants or refuses something) said? A fault is a reason the reader needs for the plot and is never given.
KNOWLEDGE. Who knows what, and when. A fault is a character who acts on something no earlier page gave them, who fails to react to something remarkable they have plainly seen, heard or been told (walking beside it without a word), or who "discovers" what the reader already saw them learn.
PLACE. Track every named character's place and the time of day page by page. A fault is a character in two places at once, a character who appears without arriving, who is forgotten mid-scene with no exit, or who leaves and is never mentioned again, or a time or weather jump the text does not explain.
CONTRADICTION. A later page contradicts an earlier one: a thing, ability or feature presented as new or surprising that already appeared; an object held by someone who no longer has it, or by two people; a number that changes; a rule of the story world broken without comment; a page that states as true what an earlier page told otherwise.
FRIEND. A friend or family member is never unkind, dismissive or careless toward the main character without a reason the pages give (a want of their own, a fear, a misunderstanding), and an unkindness is answered by a later page (an apology, a repair, or the answer the main character gives it). A conflict with a reason on the page is not a fault.
NOPROGRESS. A page where nothing changes: no new problem, try, discovery, feeling or decision, only walking, arriving or describing.
CAUSE. An event with no cause the reader can follow, or an obvious simpler solution the characters ignore with no reason ("why don't they just ...?").
VERSE. Lines where the beat stumbles so a first reader would trip, and lines that carry no story and exist only for the rhyme.

# SEVERITY

Every finding is MAJOR or MINOR.

MAJOR means a child or parent would stop the reading and ask "but why?" or "how?", or the ending would feel unearned. A finding is MAJOR when it is one of these:
- OBSTACLE: someone other than the main character makes the deciding move that removes the central problem.
- STAKES: what the main character wants or what failing costs is never said, or the driving creature's reason is never said and the plot turns on it.
- KNOWLEDGE: a character acts on knowledge no page gave them, or does not react to the very thing the plot turns on, or to something so remarkable that any child would ask why nobody says anything.
- PLACE: a character in two places at once, appearing without arriving, or vanishing from a scene that goes on.
- CONTRADICTION: a later page contradicts an earlier page on something a child who heard both would notice (a feature shown as new that was already there, an object that is in two hands, a count that changes).
- FRIEND: a friend or family member acts against the main character with no reason on the pages and no repair.
- CAUSE: the whole problem exists only because an obvious simple solution is ignored without a reason.

Everything else is MINOR: an arguable reading, a small gap the reader fills without noticing, a detail only a careful adult would catch, a style preference. NOPROGRESS and VERSE are always MINOR. When you doubt whether a finding is real, leave it out; when it is real and you doubt only the weight, weigh it by whether a listening child would ask.

# RULES

- Report only what a reader of THIS text would actually notice. Never invent a fault to fill a question.
- Do not report style, word choice, spelling or grammar. Do not ask for what a picture book leaves to its pictures (clothes, colours, the look of a place), and do not treat the page text as a checklist of facts that must all be said.
- Make-believe is allowed: a magic rule is fine as long as the book keeps to it.
- The quote is copied word for word from one page named in "pages". For a fault that is something never said (STAKES), the quote is an empty string.
- The fix is the smallest change to the words that solves the fault, written as an instruction to an editor. It changes words only: no page is added, no event is moved to another page, no plot is changed.

# OUTPUT

Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:

{"resolution": {"page": <number or null>, "actor": "<who performs the act that removes the central problem>", "byMainCharacter": <true or false>},
 "findings": [
  {"pages": [<page numbers the fault touches, the first is where it shows>], "question": "<OBSTACLE|STAKES|KNOWLEDGE|PLACE|CONTRADICTION|FRIEND|NOPROGRESS|CAUSE|VERSE>", "severity": "<MAJOR|MINOR>", "quote": "<words copied from the page, or an empty string>", "fix": "<the smallest change>"}
 ]}

A book with no fault has "findings": [].

**T1 (p2):** The line «Drinnen klemmte der Reissverschluss an Jannas Mantel» is wrong, because the coat has toggles. It changes to «Drinnen wollten die Knebel nicht zugehen». The book is told in verse, so I recast the whole page into couplets. All facts stay: the coat will not close, Janna's murmured line, her run out, the kick into the leaf pile, the silver leaf lifting, and her staring at it. The detail that the leaves flew up is dropped, because the picture shows the scattered leaves.

**T2 (p9):** Polina, Melodi and Melisa never react to Silbermond. I add one reaction before «Da bist du ja!»: Melodi and Melisa marvel, and Polina says «Ein Einhorn!». The hint for s9 is already met, because Melodi hears Polina's answering shout, which any child can hear, and then calls «Halt!». I keep that. The page is recast in couplets and every other fact stays: the row stops before the ring closes, Melisa lifts the lantern, Janna runs in beside Polina, and Silbermond walks next to her.

**Four cases for pages not named:** I found no abbreviation or acronym, no em-dash or en-dash, and no text that contradicts its outline. All other pages ship unchanged.
